title: Chapter 60: The Road to the Glass, Part 2 of 5: A Level That Does Not Exist
html:
There were fifty-three steps. Corin counted them. He did not know why. He had never been a man who counted things. But he counted them now, going down into the dark on the crutch, with Oren's fist in the back of his coat, a step at a time. Fifty-one. Fifty-two. Fifty-three.
And then the stair stopped, and there was a door.
It was small. Smaller than any door Corin had seen in the city. Round-topped, like a church window, made of black wood bound with iron, set deep into a wall of old stone that was not the Ministry's stone. Older. Rougher. Gray-green, with damp in the joints. There was no handle. There was only a keyhole, in the middle of the door, at the height of a man's chest. And round the keyhole, carved into the black wood, very fine, an oak leaf. The same leaf as the bow of the key.
There was no light. Not a lamp. Not a candle. And yet Corin could see the door quite clearly. The way you can see in a dream.
Oren could not. He stood behind Corin on the bottom step with his fist in Corin's coat and his face turned toward the door, and Corin could see in his eyes that he saw nothing at all. A stone wall, in the dark, at the bottom of a stair he could not see either.
"Is it there?" said Oren. Very low.
"It's there."
"Then open it. Before I start to think about where I'm standing."
Corin put the oak-leaf key in the keyhole.
It went in as if it had been made yesterday. Smooth. All the way. And he turned it, and it turned, with a sound like a breath let out after a long time held. And the small black round-topped door swung inward on its own, slowly, without a creak, into the dark.
Saints, said Malakor. Very quietly. Behind his left ear. Saints. It's still here.
Corin went in.
And as he went in, the room lit.
Not with fire. With the thing he had seen in the jars in the cold room of the Bourse. A faint gray light, slow, folding and unfolding, that came from nowhere and everywhere at once. From the walls. From the floor. From the low round roof. It came up as he stepped over the sill, the way the light comes up in a room when you open the curtains on a gray morning, and it showed him the room.
It was round.
Like the cold room. Like the dome. Like the glass passage. Round, and low, with a curved stone roof, and walls of the same old gray-green stone as the door. Perhaps fifteen paces across. Dry. Very dry, and very cold, and very still, with a smell of dust, and old paper, and something else, very faint, like hot metal that has long gone cold.
There was a bench along one side.
A long workbench of black wood, scarred and burned and cut, with tools laid out on it in a neat row. Small tools. Fine ones. Files and gravers and tiny hammers and pincers, and a little anvil no bigger than a fist, and a vise. And in a rack at the back of the bench, standing upright like pens in a pot, rods.
Silver rods.
A dozen of them. Long and thin, the length of a forearm. Some of them finished, polished, with a spiral cut down the length of them, fine as a thread. Turning right. All of them turning right. And some of them not finished. Plain silver, with the spiral only begun. And one, at the end, with the spiral cut halfway down and then stopped. As if the hand cutting it had been called away and never come back.
Mine, said Malakor. All mine. Every one. A pause. That last one. I was cutting that one the night they came to tell me about the Glass.
There was a desk.
Small. Against the far wall. With a chair pushed back from it, as if somebody had stood up in a hurry. Papers on it. A great many papers, in drifts, curling at the edges, gray with dust. An inkwell, dry, with a crust of black at the bottom. A pen, lying across the papers, where it had been put down.
There was a cot.
Narrow. Iron. Against the wall by the door. With a thin mattress, and a pillow, and a blanket folded on the end of it. A gray blanket. Old. Coarse wool.
Corin looked at the blanket.
And stopped.
He did not know why. He stood in the middle of the round room with the gray light folding and unfolding round him and Oren's fist in the back of his coat, and looked at a folded gray blanket on the end of an iron cot, and could not move.
A boy of ten, small for it, in a gray blanket, in a cold room.
He had seen it. In the stone. Through Lord Thorne's eyes, through Linus's face, coming in at the study door with his stick. And Elara—
No. Not Elara. He had not seen anything through Elara's eyes. He did not know why he had thought her name.
But he knew the blanket.
Not with his head. With the rest of him. His hands knew it. His shoulders knew it. The back of his neck knew it, where the rough wool would have scratched. He had been wrapped in that blanket. On that cot. In this room. When he was ten years old and small for it, and had nothing in him. And an old man's voice had said, There. There, now. I can't give you back what they took. But I'll give you this instead.
Linus brought you here, said Malakor. Very quietly. After. Corvell was dead by then. Linus was the only one left who had the key. He brought you down here, in the dark, the night they gave you to him, and sat with you on that cot for three days. And made you kind. A long pause. I watched him. From the rod. He'd brought the rod down with him. It was in his pocket. I watched him do it, and I thought he was a fool. And I was wrong.
Corin went to the cot.
He did not sit on it. He put his gray-gloved hand on the folded blanket. Just laid it there. On the rough wool.
He could not feel it. Not through the black fingertips. But he could feel it through his palm. A little. Like through a glove.
It was enough.
"What is this place?" said Oren behind him. His voice was very strange. "Vane. I can see it now. The room. I couldn't on the stair. I can see it now."
Corin turned round.
Oren had let go of his coat. He was standing just inside the round-topped door, looking at the bench, and the rods, and the desk, and the cot. His face had gone white under the gray beard.
"It knows you," said Corin. He did not know how he knew it. "It's letting you see it. Because you came in holding on to me."
Like the glass, said Malakor. Like the glass passage under the Bourse. Who do you think the Lady's mother learned that from?
Corin went to the desk.
Bottom of the pile, said Malakor. On the left. Under the ink stain shaped like a hare. One sheet. The old letters. My hand.
There was an ink stain shaped like a hare. On the corner of the desk. Old, and brown, and faded, a long-eared shape running. Corin moved the drifts of gray dusty paper aside, carefully, with the sides of his gloved hands, and the dust went up in a slow cloud in the gray light and settled again. Under it all, at the bottom, on the left, under the hare, there was a sheet.
One sheet. Thick, yellow, soft at the edges. Written close on both sides in the curling, looping old letters with the marks above and below them like birds on a wire. The same letters as the back of Linus's book.
Corin picked it up.
Read it to him, said Malakor. To the captain. Out loud. He should hear it. He's going where you're going. A pause. Say it after me.
And Corin read it.
In the round room under the Ministry, in the gray light that folded and unfolded, with Oren standing just inside the door and the silver rods in their rack on the bench and the gray blanket on the cot. Word by word. After the dry old voice behind his left ear. In a voice that was Fenton's, and not quite his own.
"To whoever opens this door, if anybody ever does.
"My name was Malakor. I was the first of the Ash-Harvesters, or the first they wrote down, which is not the same. This was my room. I worked here for forty years. I made the rods, and wrote the slow ways, and taught Corvell, and he will teach whoever comes after.
"Tonight I am going away. I do not think I will come back.
"They came to me this evening, three of them, from the Council, with a paper. They told me that a village in the north, in the hills above the Glass, has burned. They told me it was the fever. I have been to that village. There was no fever. There was never any fever. I know what was there. I have known for twenty years. I helped to hide it."
Corin stopped.
He looked at the page.
Go on, said Malakor. Go on, boy. Don't stop. If you stop, I'll stop. And I won't be able to start again.
Corin went on.
"I cannot write here what was there. I have folded it. In myself. Tonight, before I go. So that if they take me, and they will try, they will find a crease where it should be.
"But I will not let it be lost. So I have written it all. Everything. What was in the village. Who. Why. What the man with the gentle voice wanted with them, and what he did, and where he took the ones he did not burn. I have written it in my journal. In plain letters, so that anybody can read it. And I am taking the journal with me tonight. To the one place in the world where nothing can be burned and nothing can be taken.
"To the Glass.
"To Sola's bunker. Under the great waste she made. Where she stood at the end, sixty years ago, and burned the sun out of the sky to stop an army, and left nothing behind her but glass. I was there, with her, when I was young. I know the way. I know the door. I will leave my journal in the iron box under her map table, where she kept her orders. And I will close the box. And it will be there when I am not.
"Whoever reads this: go to the Glass. Go to the bunker. Open the box.
"And if you can, take a child of Oakhaven with you. One who got out. There will be one. There is always one. It will know the way better than you. It will not know why."
And under that, at the very bottom, smaller, in a hand that shook:
"Forgive me, Corvell. Lock the door. Give the key to somebody kind.
"M."
Corin lowered the page.
The gray light folded and unfolded round them in the round room.
Nobody said anything for a long time.
Then Oren said, very quietly, from the doorway: "A child of Oakhaven."
Corin did not answer.
"One who got out," said Oren. "That's what the stone said. In the crypt. You told her. Seven went south in the crate. Five in the vault. One dead. One got out." He was looking at Corin. Hard. The way he had looked at him in Cinder Lane. From his boots to his hair. "And you were born in Oakhaven. It's on the first page of your book."
"I know."
"And you were ten when it burned."
"I know."
"And you came out of it with nothing in you. And somebody gave you to Linus Hale." Oren did not look away. "In a gray blanket."
Corin looked down at the page in his hands.
Boy, said Malakor. Very quietly.
Is it me?
The dry old voice did not answer.
Malakor. Is it me? The one who got out?
I don't know, said Malakor.
And for the first time in six years, Corin heard the old dead harvester's voice shake.
I don't know. That's the truth. It's folded. Whatever I knew about it, I folded, the night I wrote that page. I can feel the crease. I can feel the edges of it. I can't open it. A long breath. It's in the journal. Whatever it is. In plain letters. In the iron box under Sola's map table. Under the Glass. Another breath. I'm sorry, boy. I'm so sorry. I've had six years to tell you, and I couldn't, because I didn't know I couldn't until I tried. And I've tried. Every night. And there's a crease.
Corin stood still for a long time.
Then he folded the yellow page. Not small. In half. And in half again. The ordinary way. The way you fold a letter to go in a coat pocket. And put it inside the Ledger, behind the back cover, where the oak-leaf key had been.
And took the oak-leaf key out of the lock of the small black door, as they went out.
And locked it behind them.
And went up the fifty-three steps in the dark, with Oren's fist in the back of his coat again, counting. One. Two. Three.
At the top, the fifth cupboard swung shut behind them without a sound. And Oren turned round, and looked at the end wall of the Harvesting Section, and Corin saw him count.
"Four," said Oren.
And then, after a moment, more slowly:
"No. Five." He rubbed his eyes with his good hand. "Saints. Five."
Toby was at his desk, by the cupboards, in his black coat, which smelled of burning. Eating his bun. He did not look up as they went past. But his free hand, on the green leather of his desk, was shaking.
The third bell had not yet rung.
At the door of the Harvesting Section, Corin stopped. And went back. And put his gray-gloved hand, for a moment, on Toby's shoulder. On the black coat that was too big. The way Oren put his hand on Gideon's head.
Toby went on eating his bun.
But he did not take his eyes off his ledger, and they were very bright.
Outside, in the Records yard, the brass lamp over the loading door was burning blue again. And as Corin went down the ramp past it, on the crutch, it went white, all at once, and hissed. And the clerks crossing the yard with their bundles of paper all turned round to look.
But by then he was through the gate.
Wren Comes
She came at the second bell after noon. When the Choir was singing.
Corin heard the Choir first. He was sitting by the brazier in the crypt with the folded yellow page in his lap, not reading it, only holding it, and the sound came down to him from very far off, from the top of the Hill, across the river, through the open door at the top of the twenty-three steps. High and sweet and very faint. Children's voices. A long way away. Like birds heard from the bottom of a well.
And then, over the singing, closer, feet. Running. On the frozen path through the churchyard. Light, and quick, and not stopping.
And a knock on the church door above. Three times. And then twice.
Oren was on his feet with his sword half out before the second knock. Gideon was up from beside his father. Juno, who had come back from the Ink Quarter at the second bell of the morning with her feet bleeding through the sacking and a bun in her pocket that Toby had given her, sat up on her blankets with her whistle.
Silas went up the steps.
Corin heard the door open. And a girl's voice, out of breath, very correct. And Silas's voice, very low.
And then Silas came back down the twenty-three steps. Slowly. Not looking at anybody. With his crooked spectacles in his hand.
And behind him, Wren.
She was not in her white coat. She was in a plain gray cloak, a servant's cloak, with the hood down, and her fair hair had come loose from its knot at one side and was hanging over her ear. Her face was very white. Her breath was going in and out fast, in clouds, in the cold air of the crypt. She had run all the way. From the top of the Hill. Down the Crescent and through the Old Town and over the bridge and up the lane. Two hundred and twelve.
She stopped at the bottom of the steps.
She looked round the crypt. At Oren with his sword. At Gideon and his huge gray father. At Juno. At the word in blue chalk on the floor by the fire.
And then at Corin.
"It's time," she said.
Nobody moved.
"The Inquisitor said to come," said Wren. "If it was time. Day or night. Wherever she was." She swallowed. "But she's already there. She's been there since the first bell. In the white room. With him." She looked at Corin. "So I came for you."
"For me."
"She sent me." Wren's young correct voice wavered, and steadied. "She said I was to say it exactly. She said: Tell him, not by myself."
Corin sat very still by the brazier.
Then he folded the yellow page, and put it in the Ledger, and put the Ledger in Fenton's coat. And reached for the crutch.
It took a long time to get up. It always did now. Silas did not help him. Nobody did. They knew better. He got his good leg under him, and the crutch, and his hand on the pillar, and pushed. And stood.
"How long?" he said.
"The doctor came at noon," said Wren. "He said today. He said before dark. He said—" She stopped. "He said she should send for whoever she wanted. So she sent me."
"I can't run," said Corin.
"I know."
"It's two hundred and twelve steps down the lane. And ninety-one paces on the bridge. And the whole of the Old Town. And the Hill." He did not know how he knew the numbers. He had not counted them. She had. They were in his head anyway, the way her voice was. "On this, it'll take me till the fourth bell."
"I know," said Wren. "There's a carriage."
Corin looked at her.
"At the bottom of the lane," said Wren. "By the river. The Inquisitor's own. He sent it with me. Gray, with no crest. He said it would be quicker." She looked at the floor. "He said, Tell the harvester it's not a trap. Tell him I've had two years to make traps and I've never once made one for her."
Nobody said anything.
Oren put his sword away.
"I'm coming," he said.
"The carriage only takes two," said Wren. "Inside. And the driver."
"Then I'll sit on the roof."
Wren looked at him. At the gray beard, and the sling of black shawl, and the sword. And something happened at the corner of her correct young mouth that was almost, not quite, a smile.
"Yes, Captain," she said.
Gideon was standing by the fire with his father's great gray hand in his.
Corin looked at him.
Gideon looked back. And did not say anything. And then he let go of his father's hand, and came across the crypt, in his boots with no big toes in them, and stood in front of Corin, and looked up at him. And reached inside his coat. And took out the small stub of blue chalk.
And held it out.
"For the white room," said Gideon. "In case. I don't know what you'll need to write. But you'll need something."
Corin took the chalk.
It was warm from Gideon's coat. From being next to the two jars. The small one and the bigger one, against his chest.
"I'll bring it back," said Corin.
"No you won't," said Gideon. "You're going to the Glass. Tonight. Everybody knows." He shrugged with one shoulder. "Keep it. I can get more. The porters have barrels of it."
Corin put the chalk in his pocket.
Then he went up the twenty-three steps, on the crutch, one at a time, with Wren ahead of him and Oren behind. And out into the cold. Into the churchyard. Into the high faint singing of the children at the top of the Spire, coming across the river.
The carriage was where Wren had said. At the bottom of the lane. By the river wall. Gray, and plain, with no crest on the door, and two gray horses steaming in the shafts. And on the box, wrapped in a gray cloak with the collar up, a driver Corin did not know.
Wren opened the door.
Corin got in. It took a long time. Oren lifted his bad leg in after him, without a word, and shut the door on him, and climbed up onto the roof with his good arm, and sat down there, cross-legged, behind the driver, with his sword across his knees, in the cold, like a man on the roof of a barn waiting for a flood to go down.
Wren got in on the other side, and sat opposite Corin, and knocked twice on the roof.
And the carriage went.
Fast. Faster than Corin had thought a carriage could go on those streets. Along the river. Over Lantern Bridge, under the blue lamps, with the wheels drumming on the boards. Up through the Old Town, past the end of Ferrule Street, where the oil lamp over the door of the Lamplighter's Rest was burning yellow in the day. Up the Crescent, past the corner where the Watchmen stood, who stepped back off the pavement and did not look. Past the foot of the Spire.
The Choir had stopped singing.
Corin sat in the gray carriage with his hands on the crutch across his knees and looked out of the window and did not see anything.
Wren was looking at him.
He felt it. He turned his head.
She was sitting very straight on the seat opposite, in her gray servant's cloak, with her hands in her lap, and her hair hanging loose over one ear. And she was looking at him the way she had looked at him in the hall of the plain gray house. When he said I know you.
"You said you knew me," said Wren. "Yesterday. In the hall."
"Yes."
"You said I lied for you. In the autumn. And gave you a stone."
"Yes."
"I did," said Wren.
The carriage swayed round a corner.
"I lied for you," said Wren. Very quietly. Very correctly. As if she were reading it from a report. "In the autumn. At the Ministry. They asked me if I'd seen you go down the back stair with a rod in your coat, and I said no. I had seen you. I said no." She looked at her hands. "And I gave you a stone. From the beach at the bottom of the Fish Stairs. Gray, with a white line round it. I'd had it since I was small. I don't know why I gave it to you. My hand just did it."
"I've still got it," said Corin.
Wren looked up.
"In my coat," said Corin. "The other coat. In the crypt. The Ledger says so. Wren Halloway. Bring her stone back."
Wren went very white.
"I don't want it back," she said.
"No?"
"No." Her voice had gone very small. "Keep it. Take it with you. To the Glass." She looked out of the window. At the white stone of the Spire, going past, very close. "I don't know why. I just think it ought to go there. I think it came from there. A long time ago." She stopped. "That's a stupid thing to say. It came from the beach at the bottom of the Fish Stairs."
"It's not stupid," said Corin.
The carriage turned into Steeple Lane, and slowed on the old unswept snow, and stopped.
Wren did not move to open the door.
"The fourth note," she said. Not looking at him. "Of the tune. The one I hum. I've always known three. Since I can remember. And Miss Thorne knew the fourth. She said it was her mother's." She swallowed. "And Polly, the little girl at Crown Walk, she knows a fifth. Miss Thorne told me. On the stair. This morning, when she came in." She looked at Corin. "Do you know it? The tune? Do you know any of it?"
Corin looked at her.
He opened his mouth to say no.
And something came up out of him instead. From very far down. From under the place where the Lady was, under the empty room, under everything. Something he did not know was there. He did not hum it. He could not have hummed it. But he heard it. Inside his own head. Clear. Like a bell rung under water.
Three notes.
And then a fourth.
And then, very faint, a fifth.
And then, fainter still, almost nothing, so faint he was not sure he had heard it at all, a sixth.
And then a crease.
He sat in the Inquisitor's gray carriage in Steeple Lane with his hands on his crutch and did not move.
"No," he said at last. His voice came out very strange. "No. I don't know it."
It was the first lie he had told since the dome.
He did not know why he told it.
Good, said Malakor, very quietly, behind his left ear. Good, boy. Not yet. Not to her. Not here.
Wren looked at him a moment longer.
Then she opened the carriage door.
And Corin got down, slowly, on the crutch, into the snow of Steeple Lane. And Oren climbed down off the roof. And they went up the five plain steps of the plain gray house with no knocker. And the door was already open. And Silas Kross was standing in the empty white hall, in his shirtsleeves, at the foot of the scrubbed pale stair. Waiting.
He did not say anything.
He stood aside.
